course.title: Browser Forensics
course.description: A browser-focused forensic course covering evidence scope, Chromium and Firefox profiles, history and downloads, cookies and session state, cache, bookmarks, Local Storage, IndexedDB, service workers, extensions, SQLite/WAL acquisition consistency, timestamp normalization, browser/filesystem correlation, online-content preservation, parser validation, privacy, reporting, and a complete synthetic-data final project. It is designed for students with basic operating-system, filesystem, command-line, web, and SQLite knowledge who want disciplined browser-forensics skills without using real credentials or private browsing data.
prerequisites: Basic Windows or Linux filesystem concepts
learningOutcomes: Define a defensible browser-forensics collection scope.
Identify and contextualize Chromium and Firefox profile artifacts.
Analyze synthetic history, downloads, cookies, bookmarks, cache, Local Storage, IndexedDB, service-worker, and extension evidence.
Preserve SQLite database families and interpret WAL/journal implications.
Analyze browser databases read-only and preserve integrity metadata.
Normalize browser timestamps while retaining source values and conversion context.
Correlate browser, filesystem, and other evidence without overclaiming attribution.
Validate parser functions against known synthetic artifacts.
Write evidence-grounded browser-forensic findings and closure records.
Complete the final Browser Evidence Acquisition, Correlation & Reporting Workbench.

modules.title: Browser Forensics Foundations
modules.description: Evidence model, profile boundaries, provenance, privacy, and collection scope.

lessons.title: Browser Forensics Scope and Evidence Types
lessons.description: Understand the browser evidence surface and its limits.
learningObjectives: distinguish application state from direct user action
map investigative questions to browser and corroborating evidence

notes.text: Evidence classes

Browser evidence can include history, downloads, cookies, cache, bookmarks, form/search data, Local Storage, IndexedDB, service-worker data, extensions, and profile metadata. Availability varies by browser, version, platform, settings, synchronization, and retention.

items: No single browser artifact is a complete record of user behavior.
Browser artifacts are application-generated records whose semantics must be understood before interpretation.
Filesystem, operating-system, network, and provider records can corroborate browser findings.

notes.text: Do not infer intent, authorship, or complete page consumption from one browser record.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes browser history?
options: It is one artifact class among several browser evidence sources.
It proves human intent.
It is a complete audit trail.
It identifies the person at the keyboard.
quiz.answer: It is one artifact class among several browser evidence sources.
quiz.explanation: History is useful evidence but does not by itself prove intent or complete viewing.

summary: Browser forensics is application- and profile-dependent.
Corroboration is central to defensible interpretation.

lessons.title: Profiles, Scope, and Privacy
lessons.description: Define browser profile boundaries and minimize collection of unrelated data.
learningObjectives: identify a browser profile and its context
define a narrow forensic collection scope
explain why cookies and saved data require strict protection

notes.text: A browser profile groups persistent user data and configuration. A forensic examiner should record browser/version, operating system, profile, acquisition time, and collection method.

items: Collection scope should follow authorization and investigative questions.
Browser profiles may contain passwords, cookies, history, personal data, and application state.
Derived reports should minimize unnecessary personal content.

notes.text: Do not publish or replay live authentication/session material.

quiz.question: Why should browser collection be narrowly scoped?
options: Browser profiles can contain extensive unrelated personal and authentication data.
It proves human intent.
It is a complete audit trail.
It identifies the person at the keyboard.
quiz.answer: Browser profiles can contain extensive unrelated personal and authentication data.
quiz.explanation: Narrow scope reduces unnecessary exposure and preserves relevance.

summary: Profile identification prevents mixing data from different browser users or profiles.
Privacy is part of forensic quality.

lessons.title: Evidence Integrity and Provenance
lessons.description: Build an evidence intake record that links browser artifacts to acquisition context.
learningObjectives: record evidence identifiers and source paths
differentiate original evidence from derived outputs

notes.text: Minimum intake fields

items: Evidence ID and description
Browser, version, OS, and profile
Acquisition method/date/time/timezone
File list and SHA-256
Working-copy location
Tool/version and relevant limitations

notes.text: Evidence ID → Source → Acquisition → Hash → Working copy → Analysis → Report
A matching hash supports byte integrity; it does not prove authorship or intent.

practicals.title: Hash a Synthetic Browser Profile
practicals.description: Demonstrate integrity verification with synthetic browser files.
steps: Create synthetic History and Cookies files.
Copy the files to a working directory.
Modify one working copy and calculate its new digest.
practicals.solution:
```python
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib, shutil

def sha256(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()

source = Path("profile")
working = Path("working")
working.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for p in source.iterdir():
    if p.is_file():
        shutil.copy2(p, working / p.name)
        print(p.name, sha256(p), sha256(working / p.name))
```
practicals.output: Untouched source and working-copy digests should match; modifying the working copy changes its digest.

summary: Provenance connects derived findings back to source evidence.
Integrity and provenance are complementary controls.

tasks.title: Create a Browser Evidence Question Matrix
tasks.description: Map browser questions to artifacts and corroboration.
tasks.problemStatement: A case asks whether a workstation visited a service, downloaded a file, and retained related site state. Build a matrix mapping five questions to browser and non-browser evidence.
tasks.hint: Start with history, downloads, cookies, filesystem, and service/network evidence.
tasks.solutionCode: Example mappings should distinguish navigation, file acquisition, session state, timing, and attribution.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task demonstrates question-driven collection planning.

modules.title: Chromium and Chrome Family Artifacts
modules.description: Profile structure, history/download data, cookies, cache, bookmarks, and Local Storage.

lessons.title: Chromium User Data and Profiles
lessons.description: Understand Chromium user-data directory and profile concepts.

notes.text: Chromium maintains user data in a user-data directory containing one or more profiles. The path depends on operating system and installation.
Never assume the first or default profile is the relevant user profile.

quiz.question: Why record the exact Chromium profile?
options: Different profiles can contain different browser state and users.
It proves human intent.
It is a complete audit trail.
It identifies the person at the keyboard.
quiz.answer: Different profiles can contain different browser state and users.

summary: Profile paths are contextual metadata.

lessons.title: Chromium History and Downloads
lessons.description: Analyze synthetic history/download records and correlate them with files.
learningObjectives: correlate download metadata with filesystem evidence

notes.text: Chromium browser databases are SQLite-based. Exact schemas can vary by version, so schema inspection should precede hard-coded queries.

items: A download record and the downloaded file are separate evidence objects.
Corroborate target path/name, timing, and content hash when available.

notes.text: A URL visit/download record does not automatically prove a human manually initiated the action.

practicals.title: Query a Synthetic Chromium Database
practicals.description: Inspect a synthetic browser database read-only.
steps: Open the DB with a read-only connection.
practicals.solution:
```python
import sqlite3, csv
con = sqlite3.connect("file:History?mode=ro", uri=True)
print(con.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' ORDER BY name").fetchall())
rows = con.execute("SELECT url, title, visit_time FROM urls ORDER BY visit_time DESC").fetchall()
with open("history_export.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["url", "title", "visit_time"])
    w.writerows(rows)
con.close()
```
practicals.output: The output contains schema information and synthetic rows without changing the source DB.

summary: Download findings become stronger when browser and filesystem observations agree.

lessons.title: Chromium Cookies and Session State
lessons.description: Interpret cookies and protect credential-like browser state.

notes.text: Browser cookies can preserve site preferences and session state. Some may be usable as authentication material, making them sensitive forensic data.
Do not replay, publish, or test live cookies. Use synthetic records in training.

quiz.question: Why are cookies especially sensitive?
options: Some cookies can contain authentication or session-related material.
It proves human intent.
It is a complete audit trail.
It identifies the person at the keyboard.
quiz.answer: Some cookies can contain authentication or session-related material.
quiz.explanation: Session-related state can function like a credential.

summary: Cookies require both forensic and security controls.

lessons.title: Chromium Cache, Bookmarks, and Local Storage
lessons.description: Use secondary artifacts as contextual evidence.
learningObjectives: recognize Local Storage as application state

items: Cache may be evicted, replaced, or incomplete.
Bookmarks represent saved browser state, not necessarily recent use.
Local Storage can preserve origin-associated application data.

notes.text: Do not claim complete page content or recent viewing from a bookmark/cache entry alone.

quiz.question: What does a bookmark establish?
options: That the browser profile recorded a saved bookmark state.
It proves human intent.
It is a complete audit trail.
It identifies the person at the keyboard.
quiz.answer: That the browser profile recorded a saved bookmark state.
quiz.explanation: A bookmark alone does not establish recent viewing or authorship.

summary: Secondary artifacts are valuable context, but their lifecycle and semantics differ.

tasks.title: Correlate a Chromium Download
tasks.description: Correlate synthetic browser and filesystem evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Determine whether a browser download record is consistent with a file found on disk.
tasks.hint: Use more than the URL: compare target metadata and content hash where available.
tasks.solutionCode: The evidence should support a browser-recorded download plus a matching file, while leaving human intent unresolved.

modules.title: Firefox Artifacts
modules.description: Firefox profiles, Places, cookies, form history, and session data.

lessons.title: Firefox Profiles and Core Files
lessons.description: Identify important Firefox profile files.
learningObjectives: distinguish stored passwords from ordinary browser evidence

notes.text: Mozilla documents profile directories as the location for browser data such as bookmarks, downloads, browsing history, form history, cookies, session data, extensions, and preferences.

items: `places.sqlite` contains bookmarks and browsing history/download-related data.
`cookies.sqlite` contains cookie data.
`formhistory.sqlite` stores search/form autocomplete data.
`sessionstore.jsonlz4` stores current tab/window session state.

notes.text: Password files such as `key4.db` and `logins.json` can contain credential material; do not expose them in training outputs.

summary: Firefox evidence is organized by profile and artifact family.

lessons.title: Firefox Places Database
lessons.description: Analyze synthetic Places data using schema-aware queries.

notes.text: Firefox Places stores bookmarks and browsing history in a SQLite-backed database. Mozilla current profile documentation identifies `places.sqlite` as a key source.
Schemas can evolve; report the browser version and query assumptions.

practicals.title: Inspect a Firefox Places-like Database
practicals.description: Query synthetic Places data without modifying it.
steps: Record the schema and source values.
practicals.solution:
```python
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect("file:places.sqlite?mode=ro", uri=True)
print(con.execute("SELECT name, type FROM sqlite_master WHERE type IN ('table','index') ORDER BY type,name").fetchall())
for row in con.execute("SELECT url, title FROM moz_places ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20"):
    print(row)
con.close()
```
practicals.output: Exact output depends on the synthetic schema; the exercise focuses on read-only, schema-aware analysis.

summary: Schema-first analysis reduces false interpretations.

lessons.title: Firefox Cookies, Form History, and Session Data
lessons.description: Interpret Firefox stored user-state artifacts while protecting sensitive content.

items: Cookie data can include site and login state.
Form history can preserve searches or entered form values.
Session data can preserve currently open tabs/windows at the time it was written.

notes.text: Do not reproduce private searches, form values, or credentials unnecessarily in a report.

summary: Firefox artifacts answer different questions and should not be flattened into one event type.

tasks.title: Create a Firefox Artifact Note
tasks.description: Produce a source-linked note for synthetic Firefox artifacts.
tasks.problemStatement: Document the profile/version, source files, schema/fields used, findings, and three limitations.
tasks.hint: Keep original source values and distinguish storage state from user action.
tasks.solutionCode: A correct note identifies `places.sqlite`, `cookies.sqlite`, and relevant session/form artifacts with explicit limitations.

modules.title: SQLite, WAL, and Acquisition Consistency
modules.description: Read-only analysis, browser database families, WAL, journals, and live acquisition context.

lessons.title: SQLite Main Database, Journal, and WAL
lessons.description: Understand SQLite file relationships relevant to browser acquisition.
learningObjectives: identify main DB, journal, WAL, and SHM files
preserve the database family together when relevant

notes.text: SQLite documents the main database format and describes rollback journals and WAL mode. In WAL mode, the on-disk state can involve a main DB, `-wal`, and `-shm` files.

items: The WAL can contain committed transactions not yet checkpointed into the main database.
Separating a DB from its WAL can lose relevant state or produce an inconsistent view.
The acquisition state and whether the browser was running should be documented.

quiz.question: Why can an SQLite WAL matter to browser forensics?
options: The WAL can contain committed transactions not yet checkpointed into the main database.
It proves human intent.
It is a complete audit trail.
It identifies the person at the keyboard.
quiz.answer: The WAL can contain committed transactions not yet checkpointed into the main database.
quiz.explanation: The WAL is part of the database state while WAL mode is active.

summary: SQLite acquisition is a consistency problem as well as a querying problem.

lessons.title: Read-Only SQLite Analysis
lessons.description: Use read-only SQLite access and parameterized queries.
learningObjectives: verify the file hash remains unchanged

notes.text: sqlite3.connect("file:History?mode=ro", uri=True)
Python sqlite3 supports URI filenames, allowing a forensic working copy to be opened in read-only mode. Parameterized queries separate SQL logic from values.
Read-only querying does not replace acquisition/preservation controls.

practicals.title: Hash, Query, and Re-hash a Browser DB
practicals.description: Verify that read-only analysis leaves a synthetic working database unchanged.
practicals.solution:
```python
import sqlite3, hashlib
from pathlib import Path

def sha256(path):
    h=hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path,'rb') as f:
        for b in iter(lambda:f.read(1024*1024),b''):
            h.update(b)
    return h.hexdigest()

db=Path('working/History')
before=sha256(db)
con=sqlite3.connect(f'file:{db}?mode=ro',uri=True)
print(con.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM urls').fetchone())
con.close()
after=sha256(db)
print('UNCHANGED' if before==after else 'CHANGED')
```
practicals.output: A correct run should report an unchanged hash after read-only querying.

summary: Read-only access is a safety property of the analysis program, not a substitute for evidence preservation.

lessons.title: Acquisition Timing and Consistency
lessons.description: Evaluate live-browser acquisition risks for open SQLite databases.

items: An active browser may keep SQLite databases open and continue writing transactions.
Copying only the main DB can omit WAL state.
Browser process state, locks, and synchronization can affect the acquisition snapshot.

notes.text: Never improvise destructive cleanup or force-close actions on real evidence just to obtain a cleaner database.

summary: Acquisition state must be part of the evidence record.

tasks.title: Assess a Browser Database Acquisition
tasks.description: Evaluate whether a main DB-only acquisition is sufficient.
tasks.problemStatement: Compare synthetic acquisitions containing a main DB alone versus a DB with matching WAL/SHM and write a defensible assessment.
tasks.hint: Ask whether the browser was running and whether auxiliary transaction files were preserved.
tasks.solutionCode: A complete assessment identifies the DB family, acquisition state, hashes, and resulting consistency limits.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task tests acquisition reasoning rather than SQL syntax.

modules.title: Time, Correlation, and User Activity
modules.description: Browser timestamps, download correlation, search/form data, and source-preserving timelines.

lessons.title: Browser Timestamps and Normalization
lessons.description: Handle browser-specific time fields without losing source semantics.

notes.text: Browser time fields are application-specific. Different browsers and artifacts can use different epochs, units, and precisions. Verify the relevant implementation/version or parser documentation before conversion.
source_timestamp | normalized_utc | artifact | meaning | conversion_basis
Never overwrite the original browser timestamp with a converted local-time value.

summary: Time normalization is a derivation and should be auditable.

lessons.title: Downloads, File Metadata, and Corroboration
lessons.description: Correlate browser downloads with filesystem objects.
learningObjectives: use file hashes as content identifiers

items: Browser download records may identify a target filename/path or source URL depending on artifact/version.
Filesystem metadata describes file state on the local system.
A content hash can corroborate that two byte sequences match.

notes.text: Correlation does not automatically prove who initiated the download or why.

practicals.title: Correlate Synthetic Download Evidence
practicals.description: Produce a source-preserving timeline for a browser download and resulting file.
steps: Create synthetic browser and filesystem CSV records.
Normalize them without overwriting source fields.
Match download target to file path/name.
practicals.solution:
```python
import csv

events=[]
for filename,source in [('browser.csv','browser'),('filesystem.csv','filesystem')]:
    with open(filename,newline='',encoding='utf-8') as f:
        for r in csv.DictReader(f):
            events.append({'source':source,'source_time':r['timestamp'],'event':r['event'],'subject':r.get('subject',''),'details':r.get('details','')})
events.sort(key=lambda x:x['source_time'])
with open('timeline.csv','w',newline='',encoding='utf-8') as f:
    w=csv.DictWriter(f,fieldnames=['source','source_time','event','subject','details']); w.writeheader(); w.writerows(events)
```
practicals.output: The result is a derived timeline that preserves the source of each event.

summary: Browser and filesystem evidence answer different parts of the same question.

lessons.title: Search, Form, and Autofill Artifacts
lessons.description: Interpret stored user-input artifacts cautiously.

notes.text: Firefox documentation identifies `formhistory.sqlite` as a store for search-bar and form-entry information. Browser-managed form/search data can persist beyond the action that created it.
Stored data does not by itself prove a form was submitted to a site or that a person entered it at the represented time.

summary: Stored state and observed action are different forensic claims.

tasks.title: Write a Correlated Browser Finding
tasks.description: Turn synthetic browser/file data into a defensible finding.
tasks.problemStatement: Determine what is supported by a browser download record, matching file, timestamp relationship, and hash.
tasks.solutionCode: The finding should support the recorded download/file relationship while explicitly leaving human intent or physical operator identity unresolved.

modules.title: Advanced Browser Artifacts
modules.description: Cache, Local Storage, IndexedDB, service workers, extensions, and policy context.

lessons.title: Cache Evidence and Limitations
lessons.description: Use cache data as supporting context rather than a complete page record.

notes.text: Browser cache is implementation-specific and managed for performance. Entries may be evicted, replaced, validated, or stored in structures that do not reconstruct an entire page.
Do not claim complete page content solely from cache artifacts.

summary: Cache evidence must be interpreted according to browser implementation and retention behavior.

lessons.title: Local Storage and IndexedDB
lessons.description: Understand origin-scoped application state.

notes.text: Web applications may store structured state in IndexedDB and key/value data in Local Storage. Such data can persist beyond a single page visit and may be more informative than history alone.
Stored application state is not proof that a user saw or submitted the data.

summary: Origin and schema context are essential.

lessons.title: Service Workers and Offline State
lessons.description: Recognize service-worker-controlled browser state.
learningObjectives: distinguish application behavior from human action

notes.text: Service workers can intercept requests and support offline application behavior. Their registrations, caches, and associated storage can preserve application state outside the traditional history database.
Do not assign a specific action to a service worker without corroborating evidence.

summary: Modern browser behavior produces evidence outside history/download tables.

lessons.title: Extensions and Browser Policy
lessons.description: Interpret extension and configuration state.

notes.text: Browser extensions can add storage and behavior. Browser policy can also affect settings and data collection. These artifacts are contextual and version-specific.
Extension presence alone does not prove that the extension performed a particular action.

summary: Configuration evidence requires activity corroboration.

tasks.title: Analyze a Complex Browser Storage Set
tasks.problemStatement: A synthetic profile contains history, cache, Local Storage, and extension evidence. Explain what the combined evidence supports and what remains uncertain.
tasks.hint: Analyze each artifact separately before making a combined statement.
tasks.solutionCode: The conclusion should describe recorded browser/application state and explicitly avoid unsupported claims about user intent.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task tests advanced browser-artifact reasoning.

modules.title: Acquisition, Validation, Reporting, and Closure
modules.description: Live-browser collection context, online evidence, parser validation, and professional reporting.

lessons.title: Live Browser Acquisition Considerations
lessons.description: Plan acquisition when the browser is running.

items: A running browser may continue writing databases/WAL files during acquisition.
Live collection can itself change artifacts or timing.
Record whether the browser was open, logged in, syncing, or downloading.

notes.text: Do not terminate or alter a real browser session outside the documented acquisition procedure.

summary: Browser state is part of acquisition provenance.

lessons.title: Online Content Preservation
lessons.description: Preserve changing public web content when browser records are insufficient.

notes.text: SWGDE guidance addresses acquiring online content because public content can change or disappear. A defensible capture records source, acquisition time, method, and supporting context.
Public availability does not remove legal, privacy, or policy constraints.

summary: Online evidence requires temporal and source provenance.

lessons.title: Browser Parser Validation
lessons.description: Validate browser parsing with known synthetic artifacts.
learningObjectives: compare parser output to expected values

items: Build synthetic databases containing known events.
Record expected results independently.
Run the parser under the relevant browser/version conditions.
Retain expected data, tool version, output, and procedure.

summary: Validation is function- and version-specific.

lessons.title: Reporting and Case Closure
lessons.description: Produce professional browser-forensic findings and preserve reproducibility information.

notes.text: Finding pattern
Observation → Corroboration → Interpretation → Limitation → Conclusion

items: Scope/authority
Evidence inventory and hashes
Browser/profile/version
Methods/tools
Artifact findings
Timeline/correlation
Limitations
Conclusion/exhibits

notes.text: Do not include live authentication tokens or unnecessary personal browsing data in ordinary reports.

summary: A good report is traceable, cautious, and reproducible.

tasks.title: Produce a Browser Forensic Findings Report
tasks.description: Write a concise report from synthetic Chromium and Firefox evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: Include scope, evidence inventory, acquisition context, three findings, limitations, and conclusions without unsupported user attribution.
tasks.hint: For each finding identify browser, profile, source file/table, artifact meaning, and corroboration.
tasks.solutionCode: A strong report distinguishes direct observations from correlated interpretations and explicitly identifies attribution gaps.

modules.title: Final Real-World Project — Browser Evidence Acquisition, Correlation & Reporting Workbench
modules.description: Complete a realistic browser-forensics assessment using synthetic, privacy-safe evidence. This final module contains the project itself and no separate module tasks.

lessons.title: Project Architecture and Evidence Boundary
lessons.description: Design the final workbench around safe input/output separation.
learningObjectives: explain why synthetic browser data is used

items: Evidence input is treated as read-only.
Derived reports are written outside the evidence directory.
SQLite inspection is read-only.
Synthetic data avoids handling real credentials or private browsing data.

summary: Safe automation makes accidental evidence modification less likely.

lessons.title: Project Testing and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Run tests and evaluate the workbench against controlled data.

items: Use a duplicate/synthetic SQLite dataset.
Run unit tests.
Repeat an unchanged analysis and compare hashes.
Attempt an output path inside the evidence root.

summary: Passing tests validate the tested behaviors, not every browser or forensic scenario.

project.name: Browser Evidence Acquisition, Correlation & Reporting Workbench
project.description: Build a controlled-lab, read-only Python workbench that inventories synthetic browser evidence, computes SHA-256, inspects SQLite schemas, preserves source timestamps, builds timelines, and produces reproducible reports.
steps: Create synthetic Chromium History/download and Firefox Places data.
Inspect browser databases read-only and record schemas.
Create browser/filesystem timeline CSV inputs and build a source-preserving timeline.
Attempt unsafe output inside the evidence root and verify refusal.
Write a final findings note with observations, corroboration, limitations, and conclusion.

code.README.md: Browser Evidence Acquisition, Correlation & Reporting Workbench. Controlled laboratory use only; synthetic browser artifacts; no credential extraction or session replay.
code.main.py:
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse, sys
from pathlib import Path
from forensic_core import inventory

def main():
    ap=argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Read-only browser evidence inventory")
    ap.add_argument("evidence_dir",type=Path)
    ap.add_argument("--output",type=Path,default=Path("browser_report"))
    a=ap.parse_args(); root=a.evidence_dir.resolve(); out=a.output.resolve()
    if not root.is_dir():
        print("Evidence directory does not exist.",file=sys.stderr); return 2
    if out==root or root in out.parents:
        print("Refusing to write reports inside evidence directory.",file=sys.stderr); return 2
    out.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
    inventory(root,out/"file_inventory.json")
    print("Inventory written:", out / "file_inventory.json")
    return 0
if __name__=="__main__": raise SystemExit(main())
code.test_forensic_core.py:
import tempfile, unittest, sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
from forensic_core import sha256_file, list_schema

class TestCore(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_hash_and_schema(self):
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td:
            p=Path(td)/"History"
            con=sqlite3.connect(p); con.execute("create table urls(url text,title text)"); con.commit(); con.close()
            self.assertEqual(len(sha256_file(p)),64)
            self.assertIn(("urls","table"),list_schema(p))

if __name__=="__main__": unittest.main()

project.explanation: The workbench separates evidence input from derived output, uses SHA-256 for integrity, read-only SQLite access for database inspection, source-preserving timeline fields, and a strict output boundary. It is intentionally not a full forensic acquisition/parser suite and does not decrypt or replay credentials.
validationPlan: Review source to confirm evidence is not written by the tool.
limitations: It does not acquire live browser profiles.
It does not decrypt/replay cookies or passwords.
It does not parse every browser/cache format.
Generic filesystem timestamps are not browser-native timestamps.
Real cases require authorization, privacy controls, and validated forensic tooling.
